WWII and Cold War layers — Vis was closed to foreign visitors until 1989 because of the Yugoslav military installations built into and around the island's landscape; Fort George's grounds include WWII Yugoslav military positions and the network of Cold War-era tunnels that stored Tito's escape submarines

description:
Fort George stands on a limestone hilltop above Vis Town — a British Napoleonic fortification that is unlike anything else on the Dalmatian coast. Britain occupied Vis from 1811 to 1815, when the Royal Navy needed a fortified Adriatic base to maintain the blockade of French-controlled ports in the region. The island's position far into the central Adriatic — beyond the range of France's coastal garrisons in Dalmatia — made it ideal. The British built Fort George on the dominant hilltop position above the town, designed a naval anchorage at Komiža on the island's western coast, and turned Vis briefly into one of the most important British positions in the Mediterranean theatre.

The Battle of Vis (also called the Battle of Lissa) in March 1811 was fought before the fort was complete. A British squadron of four frigates and three smaller vessels, under Commodore William Hoste, met a combined French-Venetian-Italian fleet of twice its size and defeated it convincingly, securing British control of the island. Hoste's signal before the battle — 'Remember Nelson' — was a conscious echo of Trafalgar, and the victory confirmed Vis as the Royal Navy's Adriatic stronghold. Fort George was the land-based component of that strategy.

After the Napoleonic Wars, Vis passed to Austrian control and Fort George was left in varying states of maintenance. The island's modern military history is equally extraordinary: WWII saw Allied commando operations and the famous episode in which Josip Broz Tito established his headquarters in a cave on Vis while Allied aircraft protected the island (1944). During the Cold War, the Yugoslav Navy maintained Vis as a military zone, installing submarine pens, weapons caches, and command tunnels throughout the island — and closing it entirely to foreign visitors until 1989. Fort George's limestone walls sit alongside and above this Cold War infrastructure.

Today the fort is an open site with no ticket booth or formal entry fee — visitors can walk in freely during daylight hours. The GYG Land Rover tour (t425659) covers Fort George and the broader island, including the WWII submarine tunnels and the most remote beaches, with transport and guide confirmed included.
history: The island of Vis (ancient Issa) was settled by Greek colonists from Syracuse in the 4th century BC, making it one of the earliest Greek colonial settlements in the Adriatic. Roman control followed, and the island remained part of successive Dalmatian power structures through Byzantine, Venetian, and Habsburg administration. The British occupation of 1811–1815 was the first non-continental power to directly administer the island since antiquity. Fort George was constructed during this occupation as a hilltop gun battery to protect the Royal Navy anchorage in Vis harbour. After the Congress of Vienna returned the island to Austrian (and then later Yugoslav) control, the fort fell into disuse. The Yugoslav period (1945–1989) saw massive military development of the island's subterranean geography, with the Navy's secret tunnel and submarine installation network representing the most significant transformation of the island's landscape since the Venetians.
how_to_visit:
**Getting there:** Vis is accessible by catamaran or ferry from Split (catamaran: ~2 hours, ferry: ~2.5 hours). Vis Town is the main settlement, with Fort George a 15–20 minute uphill walk from the town centre along a signposted path. The GYG Land Rover tour (t425659) picks up from Vis Town and transports groups to all stops, including the fort.

**Tickets:** Fort George is a free open-air site with no ticket booth or entry charge — walk in freely during daylight hours. The GYG Land Rover island tour (t425659, from €60 per person, 4.9★ / 27 reviews) covers Fort George alongside WWII submarine tunnels, Parja Bay, remote beaches, and other island sites, with professional guide and Land Rover transport confirmed included in the tour price. This is the most comprehensive way to see Vis's full military and natural heritage in a single day.

**Practical tips:** The walk from Vis Town to Fort George is steep but takes only 15–20 minutes — wear comfortable shoes. The fort's hilltop gives better views over the harbour than any other easily accessible point on the island. After the fort, walk down to the ancient Greek remains (Issa) near the seafront — the visible foundations and the small archaeological museum document 2,400 years of continuous settlement. The island is small enough to explore extensively on a single day trip from Split.

**Combine with:** [St. Nicholas Fortress](/castles/croatia/st-nicholas-fortress) (~80 km northeast near Šibenik — the 16th-century Venetian sea fortress best experienced from a kayak, protecting the Šibenik harbour entrance) and [Kamerlengo Castle](/castles/croatia/kamerlengo-castle) (~80 km northeast in Trogir's UNESCO old town — the 15th-century Venetian fortress on the waterfront of one of Dalmatia's finest medieval towns).

faqs.question: What was Britain doing with a fortress in Croatia during the Napoleonic Wars?
faqs.answer: During the Napoleonic Wars, France controlled most of the eastern Adriatic coast — Dalmatia, Ragusa (Dubrovnik), and the Ionian Islands were under French administration or allied with Napoleon. Britain needed an Adriatic base from which the Royal Navy could blockade French-controlled ports, intercept French shipping, and project power into the eastern Mediterranean. Vis's position deep in the central Adriatic, beyond the range of French coastal garrisons, made it ideal. The Royal Navy occupied the island in 1811, commissioned Fort George on the dominant hilltop, and used it as a base for Adriatic operations until Napoleon's defeat in 1815. The 1811 Battle of Vis — a British naval victory over a much larger French fleet — secured this position.

faqs.question: Why was Vis closed to foreign visitors until 1989?
faqs.answer: After World War II, the Yugoslav People's Army turned Vis into one of the most heavily militarised islands in the Adriatic. The Navy built submarine pens and weapons storage tunnels into the island's limestone geology, installed command facilities, and stationed a permanent military garrison. The island was a classified military zone — Croatian and Yugoslav citizens from outside the military community were also restricted — and no foreign tourism was permitted. The military infrastructure was dismantled after Yugoslav dissolution began, and the island was opened to visitors in 1989. Many of the Cold War tunnels remain and are now a tourism attraction in their own right.

faqs.question: Does the GYG Land Rover tour actually go inside the WWII submarine tunnels?
faqs.answer: Yes — the GYG Land Rover island tour (t425659) includes a visit to Parja Bay and the submarine tunnel complex, which is the primary Cold War military heritage attraction on Vis. The tunnels were built to shelter Yugoslav submarines from air attack and to store weapons and supplies for the Navy's secret Adriatic operations. Parts of the tunnel network are now accessible to visitors and are included on the tour itinerary. The tour also covers Fort George, remote beaches, and other island sites over the course of a full-day programme.
